ami_style_notes:
The meeting has a relaxed, collegial academic-video-call style, with short to medium conversational turns before and after much longer, structured presentation turns. There is frequent backchanneling (“yeah,” “okay,” “great”), occasional overlap, and several false starts, repetitions, self-corrections, and audio-related interruptions, especially in informal chat and audience questions. Speakers use hedges heavily—“I think,” “sort of,” “maybe,” “you know,” “I guess,” “it could be”—even when making confident technical points, which keeps challenges indirect and collaborative rather than adversarial. Formality shifts by phase: introductions and talks are polished but still conversational, while discussion is highly informal, friendly, and exploratory. Questions are often prefaced with praise or disclaimers (“great talk,” “quick question,” “naive question”), then unfold in multi-part, somewhat winding form. Responses generally validate the question first, acknowledge uncertainty or limits, and build toward a tentative answer; participants extend one another’s ideas rather than sharply disputing them.

Meeting style for this meeting (quick_checkin): A rushed weekly check-in. People give short status updates and ask each other quick questions. Most turns are one or two sentences. Nobody summarizes. Someone has another meeting soon and the conversation stops where it stops.

Opening: Start with someone saying what they most want out of this meeting, briefly and casually.
Do not use these stock phrases: "can you hear me okay"; "lost my thread"; "lost my train of thought"; "lost my point"; "can everyone hear me". The recording does not need to begin with audio or login checks.
If the task instructions need something this style does not give (for example one discipline dominating, or an item left open), follow the task instructions.
research_problem: Testing whether financial stress narrows how people weigh present against future payoffs, and what that means for program design.

speakers.name: Dr. Aisha Rahman
speakers.background: A cognitive neuroscientist with 11 years of experience coordinating multi-site studies of stress, reward valuation, and decision-making. She has led fMRI protocol development, saliva collection logistics, cortisol assay quality control, and preregistration workflows for laboratory experiments. In this project she manages the six-month planning timeline while leading the imaging and hormone components.
speakers.distinct_perspective: Treats the laboratory manipulation as a tightly specified experimental input whose timing, control condition, and manipulation-check thresholds must be stable before neural or endocrine measures can be interpreted. She is attentive to scanner constraints, diurnal variation in saliva biomarkers, task timing, and the danger of treating a physiological correlate as evidence of a psychological construct without validated manipulation checks.
speakers.language_complexity: moderate — balances jargon with accessible language
speakers.epistemic_stance: open to other perspectives, willing to revise

speakers.name: Mateo Silva
speakers.background: A fourth-year behavioral economics PhD student with prior work on cash-transfer design, present bias, and incentive-compatible elicitation of intertemporal preferences in low-income settings. He has experience building randomized field protocols, calculating welfare-relevant outcomes, and designing payment procedures that preserve consequential choice, but has limited direct experience translating laboratory stress manipulations into program interventions.
speakers.distinct_perspective: Frames the question in terms of whether stress shifts discounting or choice under liquidity constraints in ways that alter welfare and the optimal design of payment schedules, commitment devices, or benefit timing. He is inclined to move quickly toward a field-ready treatment arm and measurable policy counterfactual, while recognizing that a credible intervention needs a reproducible laboratory basis rather than an attractive behavioral narrative alone.
speakers.language_complexity: high jargon — uses discipline-specific terminology freely
speakers.epistemic_stance: uncertain about how their methods apply to this problem

speakers.name: Priya Nanduri
speakers.background: A fifth-year social and health psychology PhD student studying financial threat, perceived scarcity, and self-regulation. She has run laboratory experiments using standardized stress inductions, validated self-report instruments, manipulation checks, and replication-oriented analysis plans. She will lead development of the financial-stress induction, neutral control, administration timing, and the pilot needed to establish whether the planned self-report stress scale detects the intended state change reliably.
speakers.distinct_perspective: Approaches financial stress as a psychological state that must be operationalized and validated before downstream behavioral or biological interpretation is warranted. She emphasizes construct validity, equivalence between treatment and control materials, prespecified manipulation-check criteria, and replication decisions rather than assuming that exposure to financial content itself constitutes stress.
speakers.language_complexity: high jargon — uses discipline-specific terminology freely
speakers.epistemic_stance: highly confident in their discipline's contribution

transcript.speaker: Mateo Silva
transcript.text: Hi—sorry, I’m a minute early for once. I mostly want to leave today knowing what laboratory result would actually be enough for us to start, uh, specifying the field arm, instead of picking a payment-timing treatment on intuition.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Aisha Rahman
transcript.text: For me, it has to be a pre-specified effect that replicates in both lab samples with the exact same induction, control, timing, and manipulation check. And if the signal is just noisier choices under stress, rather than a directional shift toward sooner payments, then I’m not sure a payment-timing field treatment is, um, interpretable. We’d need to distinguish that first.

transcript.speaker: Mateo Silva
transcript.text: Mm, right.

transcript.speaker: Priya Nanduri
transcript.text: Before we treat either choice pattern as meaningful, I need the induction to clear a prespecified manipulation check against an equivalently structured neutral control. Financial content by itself isn't the construct. Aisha, how tightly does saliva timing fix the induction-to-task interval? Would there be room for the self-report measure before scanning without compromising the assay- the assay window?

transcript.speaker: Dr. Aisha Rahman
transcript.text: The self-report can go before the scan, yes, but I’d want its timing fixed, not treated as dead time. For cortisol, we should hold a consistent induction-to-first-saliva interval and put the valuation task in that same post-induction window. I need to check whether all the scanner blocks we have can actually fit in that afternoon collection range, or, um, whether that timing works.

transcript.speaker: Priya Nanduri
transcript.text: That works, as long as we define the questionnaire as part of the induction sequence and hold that interval identically in the psychology lab. I need to check the scale's sensitivity in our intended pool before I commit to a pilot cutoff, though. The earlier irregular-income subgroup result may be, may be wording sensitivity rather than genuine moderation.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Aisha Rahman
transcript.text: Could you give me even a rough sense of how much revision you expect after the pilot? Once I map the scanner blocks against the afternoon saliva window, changing the questionnaire or- if the induction sequence changes late, we could lose comparability, not just convenience.

transcript.speaker: Priya Nanduri
transcript.text: I expect one bounded revision cycle, not an open-ended redesign. The pilot has to tell us whether the existing scale and wording clear the criterion in the intended pool. If they do, I can lock the package immediately. And if the irregular-income pattern persists, I’d first test whether it’s prompt-specific before treating it as substantive heterogeneity.

transcript.speaker: Mateo Silva
transcript.text: That bounded revision cycle helps. I’d hold off on locking any field feature until the package is locked and Aisha’s task tells us it’s an actual valuation shift, not engagement or noise. Meanwhile, I need to check whether the partners can vary disbursement timing without touching eligibility, enrollment, or perceived transfer value.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Aisha Rahman
transcript.text: That’s the right constraint. The partners need to isolate timing while holding the nominal transfer and all the enrollment rules fixed. That’s much cleaner. But if the lab result is mostly increased choice variability, I’m not sure timing is the feature we should carry forward at all.

transcript.speaker: Mateo Silva
transcript.text: Hm, that's the key distinction.

transcript.speaker: Priya Nanduri
transcript.text: For the psychology side, I'd want to interpret the directional choice effect only after the state manipulation itself replicates. Otherwise, the variability could just reflect different comprehension or disengagement. Mateo, when you say a feature other than timing, what program levers can the partners realistically—

transcript.speaker: Mateo Silva
transcript.text: The most plausible one is timing, an earlier versus later tranche with total value held fixed. If the effect ends up looking more like difficulty executing future-oriented choices, then maybe, maybe a voluntary commitment option or a protected later tranche. But I honestly don't know whether partners can administer that without it feeling like a reduction in choice, so I'm checking. I don't think we have a credible lever for generic noise.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Aisha Rahman
transcript.text: I’d be cautious about calling a protected later tranche the lab translation unless the task effect is specifically on future-value weighting. If it’s just- if it’s more inconsistent responding, that’s different. Mateo, could your partner check whether a voluntary version is operationally possible? That distinction may matter a lot for what we pre-specify.

transcript.speaker: Mateo Silva
transcript.text: I’ll ask specifically about a voluntary protected tranche, with opt-in rather than default enrollment, and whether they can implement it without changing the participant-facing value of the transfer. But I’d keep that as a feasibility contingency, not pre-specify it as the field arm yet. The lab pattern has to tell us whether there’s actually a future-value mechanism to translate.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Aisha Rahman
transcript.text: Okay, that’s useful.

transcript.speaker: Priya Nanduri
transcript.text: That gives us a clean decision rule on our side too. We don't move to a field translation from a lab pattern unless the manipulation check replicates and the choice result is directional, rather than just elevated inconsistency. The protected-tranche idea may be useful later, but I wouldn't let whether it's feasible pull us into reading ambiguous lab behavior as future-value weighting.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Aisha Rahman
transcript.text: Yeah—keep that as the threshold; otherwise the imaging result won’t rescue the interpretation.

transcript.speaker: Mateo Silva
transcript.text: Yeah, I think so.

transcript.speaker: Priya Nanduri
transcript.text: Yes—otherwise we are reverse-engineering the mechanism from an ambiguous outcome.

transcript.speaker: Mateo Silva
transcript.text: I think that’s enough for today—the rest can wait until next week. Thanks, both.

transcript.speaker: Priya Nanduri
transcript.text: All right. Take care, both.
